extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys), parties/respondents in USPTO/OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing practitioner conduct before the USPTO and criteria for evaluating misconduct and imposing sanctions in USPTO disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation; reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101, 11.103, 11.104)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. § 11.101, a practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client. Rules at 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.103 and 11.104 require a practitioner to provide competent representation and to act with “reasonable diligence and promptness” when representing clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures that support a violation include not promptly notifying a client of filing irregularities, failing to consult with the client about how to address irregularities, filing patent applications late, claiming wrong priority dates, allowing an application to be abandoned for failure to pay fees, failing to file required petitions (e.g., to restore priority), and failing to take steps to address errors or inform the client until much later. These factual examples (filing three applications late, loss of priority date due to late drawing, failing to respond to Notices to File Missing Parts, not filing petition to revive) are used as evidence of incompetence/lack of diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements to tribunals and failure to correct misapprehension (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.303, 11.801(a) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801 prohibits a practitioner from knowingly making a false statement of material fact, or knowingly failing to disclose a fact necessary to correct a known misapprehension, in connection with a disciplinary matter. 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) and (3) prohibit knowingly making a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal and offering evidence known to be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples supporting violations: fabricating and presenting forged emails as evidence; making affirmative oral or written statements to the BBO or OED that the practitioner knows are false; failing to identify or produce facts showing that claimed oral notifications occurred. The ALJ’s credibility findings (rejecting unsupported testimony absent corroborating dates/facts) are relied on to support these violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) states it is professional misconduct for a practitioner to “engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct such as fabricating emails, lying to one’s law firm, lying to disciplinary bodies (BBO, OED), and misleading a client about the status of patent matters (e.g., repeatedly assuring client 'no big deal' while doing nothing) constitute violations. The decision cites precedent (In re Fuess; In re Schwedler; state cases) supporting that such dishonest statements and misrepresentations breach §11.804(c). Even if some particular asserted instances (e.g., asking a client to support false story) lack record support, other undisputed dishonest acts suffice to find a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business transactions with clients — informed consent/written disclosure (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.108(a) prohibits a practitioner from entering into a business transaction with a client or acquiring an interest adverse to a client unless: (1) the transaction and its terms are fair and reasonable and fully disclosed in writing in a way the client can reasonably understand; (2) the client is advised in writing that he should seek independent legal counsel and has a reasonable opportunity to do so; and (3) the client gives informed consent in writing to the essential terms of the transaction and the practitioner’s role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting equity or other business interests from a client in exchange for legal services counts as a 'business transaction' triggering the written disclosure and informed consent obligations. The decision treats failure to disclose risks or obtain written informed consent (e.g., a lawyer who took a 5% ownership interest without such disclosures) as a violation of §11.108(a). The ALJ and precedent require practitioners to explain how the transaction may affect professional judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest rules (37 C.F.R. § 10.62)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. § 10.62, except with the consent of a client after full disclosure, a practitioner shall not accept employment if the exercise of the practitioner’s professional judgment on behalf of the client will be or reasonably may be affected by the practitioner’s own financial, business, property, or personal interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must vigilantly scrutinize business relationships to ensure representation is not accepted where their professional judgment could be affected. Accepting employment from a client without disclosure of how one’s interests might affect judgment violates §10.62 (even if no actual profit results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Business transactions/conflicting interests rule (37 C.F.R. § 10.65)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 10.65 provides that, unless the client has consented after full disclosure, a practitioner shall not enter into a business transaction with a client if they have differing interests therein and if the client expects the practitioner to exercise professional judgment therein for the protection of the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a practitioner’s and client’s interests diverge in a transaction and the client expects the practitioner to exercise judgment, the practitioner must not enter into the transaction without proper disclosure and consent. Failure to do so has been disciplined in USPTO and state precedent (cases cited in the decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent procedural obligations (priority, missing parts, fees, petitions to revive; 37 C.F.R. § 1.78(b) referenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent prosecution obligations include filing required parts timely (e.g., drawings), claiming correct priority dates, paying required fees within statutory periods (e.g., full U.S. basic national filing fee within 30 months), responding to Notices To File Missing Parts, and filing required petitions (e.g., under 37 C.F.R. § 1.78(b) to restore provisional benefit) or petitions to revive abandoned applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely file drawings or required parts can forfeit claimed provisional priority; filing an application more than a year after a provisional requires a petition under §1.78(b) to restore priority. Failure to pay fees or respond to missing parts notices can result in abandonment; failing to file a petition to revive an abandoned application is a separate culpable omission. These procedural missteps are concrete examples used to show lack of competence/diligence in disciplinary evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors for exclusion/suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(1)-(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: An ALJ initial decision that imposes exclusion or suspension must explain the reason for imposing such a sanction after consideration of: (1) whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner’s misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ must analyze these four factors and explain why a particular sanction (e.g., exclusion) is appropriate. The decision here applied the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions and weighed aggravating and mitigating circumstances before concluding exclusion was appropriate, noting intentional fabrication and significant harm (loss of client intellectual property rights) as central considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction remedies and administrative orders (post-discipline duties & prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical administrative remedies/orders following discipline include exclusion from practice before the USPTO; notice of public discipline to state disciplinary agencies and courts (37 C.F.R. § 11.59); dissociation of the practitioner's name from any USPTO Customer Number(s) and verified electronic system accounts; prohibition on applying for or obtaining a USPTO Customer Number until reinstated; and compliance with duties of disciplined practitioners under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions will often spell out operational effects of exclusion (loss of access, notification obligations, and restrictions on reapplying for customer numbers) and require compliance with post-discipline obligations. These are presented as mandatory orders in the culminating section of a sanction decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration and judicial review timelines and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Any request for reconsideration of the Director’s decision must be filed within twenty (20) days from entry of the decision pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c). If reconsideration is not filed, a disciplined practitioner may seek judicial review on the record in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 within thirty (30) days after the order recording the Director’s action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural compliance with these timelines and proper service (addresses and counsel listed) is required for appellate review or requests for reconsideration. The decision provides the addresses and service instructions for filing and serving a reconsideration request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to ALJ credibility findings on review
rubrics_metrics.description: When findings are based on determinations regarding the credibility of witnesses, reviewing bodies give even greater deference to the trial court's findings because the trial judge has the advantage of observing demeanor and tone and is better positioned to judge credibility (citing Anderson v. City of Bessemer and related authorities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review will generally not overturn credibility findings unless internally inconsistent or clearly erroneous; uncontradicted admissions (e.g., admissions of fabricating emails) greatly support credibility-based findings. The decision relies on this doctrine to sustain the ALJ’s adverse credibility determinations and resultant factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards and case precedent in sanctioning and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ALJ and Director may consider the American Bar Association’s Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions and prior USPTO and state disciplinary precedents when assessing appropriate sanctions and interpreting misconduct rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision explicitly references ABA standards and multiple USPTO and state cases (e.g., In re Lane; In re Haley; In re Watkins; In re Fuess; In re Schwedler) to support findings of misconduct and to guide selection of sanction (e.g., reprimand, suspension, exclusion). Aggravating/mitigating factors are weighed under those frameworks.
